extracted_claims.text: Under Article 53 of the EU AI Act, providers of general-purpose AI models must maintain technical documentation, make it available to authorities and downstream AI system providers, put in place a copyright policy, and publish a public summary of training data; open-source GPAI models are exempt from some documentation requirements unless classified as having systemic risk.
Under Article 53(1)(d), use of the Commission's official template to summarise training content is mandatory for GPAI model providers.

Article 55 imposes additional obligations on providers of GPAI models with systemic risk, including evaluating models using standardised protocols, assessing and mitigating systemic risks, reporting serious incidents, and ensuring cybersecurity; such providers may rely on codes of practice or harmonised standards to demonstrate compliance.
GPAI models trained with more than 10^25 FLOPs are presumed to carry systemic risk and face additional obligations such as adversarial testing.

Chapter V of the EU AI Act creates a two-tier framework for GPAI models: core obligations for all GPAI models (transparency, technical documentation, copyright compliance) effective from August 2, 2025, and additional obligations for systemic-risk models.

GPAI model provider obligations under the AI Act came into effect in August 2025, with the adoption of harmonised standards expected in August 2027 or later; the Code of Practice serves as an interim compliance tool during that period.
The European Commission released the General-Purpose AI Code of Practice on 10 July 2025 to provide operational guidance for GPAI model providers, particularly ahead of binding regulatory deadlines.
On July 18, 2025, the European Commission published guidelines clarifying the scope of GPAI provider obligations under the AI Act, complementing the GPAI Code of Practice.
The GPAI Code of Practice introduces a standardized Model Documentation Form covering training data sources, intended use cases, and licensing information to meet AI Act transparency requirements.
The Code of Practice, though not legally binding, allows GPAI providers to demonstrate compliance with the AI Act.
If an existing GPAI model is modified or fine-tuned, Article 53 obligations apply only to the modification, and Article 55 systemic-risk obligations apply only in specified cases.

On January 23, 2025, President Trump issued Executive Order 14179, 'Removing Barriers to American Leadership in Artificial Intelligence,' which revoked the prior administration's AI policies and directed agencies to remove barriers to US AI leadership.

In July 2025, the White House released 'Winning the AI Race: America's AI Action Plan,' a non-binding, voluntary policy document (not legislation) outlining more than 90 federal policy actions across three pillars: accelerating innovation, building infrastructure, and international diplomacy/security.
The AI Action Plan was issued pursuant to and in accordance with Executive Order 14179.

On December 11, 2025, President Trump signed an Executive Order titled 'Ensuring a National Policy Framework for Artificial Intelligence,' aiming to establish a uniform, minimally burdensome federal AI standard and to preempt state AI laws, with limited exceptions such as child safety protections and AI infrastructure.

The December 2025 EO directs development of federal legislative recommendations to preempt the patchwork of state AI laws, except in discrete areas including child safety protections and AI compute/data center infrastructure.

The December 2025 EO directs the Attorney General to establish an AI Litigation Task Force within 30 days to identify and challenge state AI laws inconsistent with the administration's 'minimally burdensome' policy.
The December 2025 EO also directs actions including launching a Federal Communications Commission-related initiative to challenge conflicting state AI laws.

The NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF), published January 26, 2023 by the US Commerce Department's NIST, is a voluntary, non-binding framework to help organizations identify and manage AI risks and promote trustworthy AI; it is not a binding foundation-model-specific regulation.
The NIST AI RMF is organized around four core functions: Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage.

NIST's draft document AI 800-1, 'Managing the Risk of Misuse for Dual-Use Foundation Models,' issued by NIST's AI Safety Institute, identifies voluntary risk-management practices specifically for dual-use foundation model developers, including seven objectives for managing misuse risk and transparency recommendations.
The October 2023 Executive Order on Safe, Secure, and Trustworthy AI (prior administration) referenced the NIST AI RMF, but this EO was revoked by EO 14179 in January 2025.

Unlike the EU AI Act's binding legal obligations on foundation model (GPAI) providers, current US federal AI policy (EO 14179, the AI Action Plan, NIST AI RMF, and NIST AI 800-1) consists of executive orders and voluntary guidance documents rather than enacted legislation imposing binding compliance obligations on foundation model providers.

report:
# EU AI Act Foundation Model Requirements vs. US Federal AI Policy: A Comparative Analysis

## Executive Summary
The EU AI Act imposes binding, legally enforceable obligations on providers of general-purpose AI (GPAI) models, including technical documentation, training-data transparency, and enhanced requirements for systemic-risk models (high confidence). By contrast, current US federal AI policy relies on executive orders, voluntary frameworks, and non-binding guidance rather than enacted legislation targeting foundation model providers directly (medium confidence). The most recent US development—a December 2025 executive order—seeks to preempt state AI laws in favor of a "minimally burdensome" federal approach, signaling a deregulatory trajectory distinct from the EU's compliance-focused regime (medium confidence).

## Key Findings

### EU AI Act: Binding Obligations for GPAI Providers
Under Article 53 of the EU AI Act, GPAI model providers must maintain technical documentation, share it with authorities and downstream providers, adopt a copyright policy, and publish a public summary of training data, using the Commission's official template; open-source models receive partial exemptions unless classified as systemic risk (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-53), [Digital Strategy](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/faqs/template-general-purpose-ai-model-providers-summarise-their-training-content)). Providers of GPAI models deemed to carry systemic risk face additional duties under Article 55, including standardized model evaluation, risk mitigation, incident reporting, and cybersecurity measures, with compliance demonstrable via codes of practice or harmonised standards (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-55)). One source suggests models trained above 10^25 FLOPs are presumed systemic-risk, though this claim carries low confidence and limited corroboration ([Glocert International](https://www.glocertinternational.com/resources/guides/eu-ai-act-gpai-and-foundation-model-compliance)). Modified or fine-tuned models trigger Article 53 obligations only for the modification itself, with Article 55 applying in specified circumstances (medium confidence) ([Digital Strategy FAQ](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/faqs/general-purpose-ai-models-ai-act-questions-answers)).

### Implementation Timeline and Interim Guidance
Core GPAI obligations took effect in August 2025, with harmonised standards not expected until August 2027 or later, and the Commission's GPAI Code of Practice serves as an interim compliance mechanism that, while not legally binding, allows providers to demonstrate AI Act compliance (medium confidence) ([AI Act EU](https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/introduction-to-code-of-practice)). The specific claim that the Code of Practice was released on July 10, 2025 carries only low confidence given limited corroboration (low confidence) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General-Purpose_AI_Code_of_Practice)). Supplementary Commission guidelines clarifying GPAI scope reportedly followed on July 18, 2025, though this specific date is likewise low confidence (low confidence) ([WilmerHale](https://www.wilmerhale.com/en/insights/blogs/wilmerhale-privacy-and-cybersecurity-law/20250724-european-commission-issues-guidelines-for-providers-of-general-purpose-ai-models)).

### US Federal Approach: Executive Orders and Voluntary Frameworks
President Trump's January 2025 Executive Order 14179 revoked prior administration AI policies and directed agencies to remove barriers to US AI leadership (medium confidence) ([McDermott Will & Emery](https://www.mcdermottlaw.com/insights/new-executive-order-shifts-us-ai-policy-toward-national-security)). This was followed by the non-binding "Winning the AI Race: America's AI Action Plan" in July 2025, outlining over 90 voluntary policy actions (medium confidence) ([Holland & Knight](https://www.hklaw.com/en/insights/publications/2025/07/americas-ai-action-plan-whats-in-whats-out-whats-next)). Most significantly, a December 11, 2025 executive order seeks to establish a uniform, minimally burdensome federal AI standard and preempt state AI laws except for narrow exceptions like child safety and infrastructure, and directs development of federal legislative recommendations toward that end (medium confidence) ([Sidley Austin](https://www.sidley.com/en/insights/newsupdates/2025/12/unpacking-the-december-11-2025-executive-order), [Moore & Van Allen](https://www.mvalaw.com/data-points/president-trump-takes-aim-at-state-artificial-intelligence-regulation-with-limited-exceptions)). Separately, a report that the order directs the Attorney General to establish an AI Litigation Task Force within 30 days to challenge inconsistent state AI laws rests on a single, lower-authority source and is treated as low confidence (low confidence) ([Cloud Security Alliance](https://labs.cloudsecurityalliance.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/CSA_research_note_whitehouse-national-ai-policy-framework-enterprise-security_20260411-csa-styled.pdf)).

The NIST AI Risk Management Framework, published January 2023, remains the primary federal risk-management tool—voluntary, organized around Govern/Map/Measure/Manage functions, but not foundation-model-specific regulation (low confidence) ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.15229v1), [Collibra](https://www.collibra.com/blog/the-ai-risk-management-framework-nist-ai-rmf-for-models-and-agents-with-implementation-steps)). NIST's draft AI 800-1 addresses dual-use foundation models specifically but remains voluntary guidance (low confidence) ([HLC](https://www.hlc.com/en/publications/nist-and-ntia-publish-key-resources-on-ai-risk-management-and-safety)).

### Core Distinction
Unlike the EU's binding legal obligations, US federal policy consists of executive orders and voluntary guidance without enacted legislation imposing compliance duties on foundation model providers (medium confidence) ([McDermott](https://www.mcdermottlaw.com/insights/new-executive-order-shifts-us-ai-policy-toward-national-security), [Holland & Knight](https://www.hklaw.com/en/insights/publications/2025/07/americas-ai-action-plan-whats-in-whats-out-whats-next)).

## Contradictions & Uncertainties
No direct contradictions were identified between sources. However, several claims carry low confidence (below 0.4) and warrant caution: the 10^25 FLOP systemic-risk threshold, the Code of Practice's exact release date, the Commission's July 18 guidelines date, the AI Litigation Task Force detail, and NIST AI 800-1 specifics.

## Knowledge Gaps
No source identifies a binding US federal statute directly regulating foundation models comparable to EU Articles 53/55. The eventual content and passage likelihood of federal preemption legislation called for by the December 2025 EO remains unclear. Specific EU enforcement penalties for non-compliance are not detailed, nor are comparable US enforcement mechanisms. The interaction between federal preemption efforts and existing state laws (e.g., California, Colorado) beyond stated exceptions is unaddressed, as is NIST AI 800-1's finalization status.
